evidence.quote: svr.rbf was trained and used for the prediction of the yield strength of HEAs at room at 20°C, 600°C or 800°C. A cross-validation approach was also used for pretesting of the svr.rbf algorithm.

Since the size of the initial dataset was rather small (30–35 alloys, depending on temperature), it was important to choose the optimal ratio of the new-forming training and test datasets in all used algorithms to attain the best accuracy of the prediction.
The optimal size of the training dataset was defined at 0.7 of the whole initial datasets.
A total of 50 bootstrap datasets with a size of 0.7 of the initial datasets, each created by choosing random alloys from the initial dataset

machine_learning_models.task: yield strength prediction of high-entropy alloys
machine_learning_models.validation: train/test split; bootstrap with replacement using 50 datasets of size 0.7

evidence.quote: seven well-known machine learning algorithms [68], such as a ridge regression algorithm (rid), support vector regressions with a linear kernel (svr.lin), a polynomial kernel (svr.poly), and a radial basis function kernel (svr.rbf), a regression tree algorithm (tree) and a k-nearest neighbor algorithm (knn) were compared.
Among two algorithms showing the minimum prediction error (svr.rbf and rid; Figure 4), svr.rbf was trained and used for the prediction of the yield strength of HEAs at room at 20°C, 600°C or 800°C.
